# Quickshell Pi Agent Skill Architecture

## Core Principle

> **Skills should make the LLM distrust its own knowledge and always verify against live source.**

Static doc snapshots are stale the moment they're taken. For fast-moving projects like Quickshell, a stale reference file produces confident wrong answers instead of uncertain ones. The correct mental model is:

- Here's what I know that's **specific to your setup** (never in any doc)
- Here's what I'm **likely wrong about** (version traps, renamed APIs, breaking changes)
- Here's **exactly where to fetch current truth** before answering

---

## Why Skill-Seeker-Style Tools Are Wrong By Design

Tools that crawl docs, snapshot them, and feed them to an LLM as ground truth are solving the wrong problem. They fix LLM knowledge staleness by adding more potentially-stale knowledge — just with a fresher timestamp.

The snapshot is stale the moment it's taken. And worse than not knowing something, the LLM now *confidently* knows the wrong thing because a skill file told it so.

**Skill as epistemic guardrails** (correct) vs **skill as knowledge injection** (wrong).

---

## Pi Agent Customization Layers

Pi has three distinct customization layers that serve different purposes:

| Layer | How Triggered | Code? | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Skill** | Description match or `/skill:name` | No | Stack gotchas, distrust notices, live fetch URLs |
| **Prompt Template** | `/qs <task>` | No | Repeatable session starters, context priming |
| **Extension** | Always-on TypeScript module | Yes | Live doc fetching tool, system prompt injection, LLM-callable tools |

---

## File Structure

```
~/.pi/agent/
├── skills/
│   └── quickshell/
│       └── SKILL.md
├── prompts/
│   └── qs.md
└── extensions/
    └── quickshell/
        └── index.ts
```

---

## Layer 1 — Skill

**`~/.pi/agent/skills/quickshell/SKILL.md`**

```markdown
---
name: quickshell
description: Use when working with Quickshell, QML components, PanelWindow,
  ShellRoot, ToplevelManager, Hyprland IPC in Quickshell, dock building,
  LiquidGlass widget, or any Quickshell-based desktop shell development.
---

# Quickshell — Stack Reference

## ⚠ Distrust Notice
Your training data on Quickshell is likely stale or wrong. Before writing
any Quickshell code, call the fetch_qs_docs tool to get current API info
for the types involved. Do not guess property names or signal signatures.

## Known Gotchas
- wayland.appId vs windowClass: Wayland windows use wayland.appId,
  XWayland windows use windowClass. Never mix them.
- Reactivity: use `property var foo` not plain `var foo`. Plain var
  breaks binding propagation silently.
- ToplevelManager: iterate via .values, not as a plain array.
- Flatpak appIds: reverse-domain format e.g. org.mozilla.firefox.
- XMind must be forced XWayland via --ozone-platform=x11.
- hyprctl notify instead of notify-send in this stack.

## Your Stack
- Hyprland Lua config, Omarchy-based, ~/.config/hypr/
- Never reference hyprland.conf
- Tokyo Night Midnight theme
- LiquidGlass.qml reusable widget pattern
- Quickshell dock with proximity magnification

## Live Docs
If fetch_qs_docs is unavailable, fetch manually:
https://quickshell.outfoxxed.me/docs/types/<TypeName>
```

---

## Layer 2 — Prompt Template

**`~/.pi/agent/prompts/qs.md`**

```markdown
---
description: Start a Quickshell/QML session with live doc fetching enabled
argument-hint: "[component or task]"
---
I'm working on my Quickshell dock (Hyprland, Tokyo Night Midnight, LiquidGlass
pattern). Before writing any QML, use fetch_qs_docs to verify the current API
for any Quickshell types involved.

Task: ${1:-describe what you need}
```

---

## Layer 3 — Extension

**`~/.pi/agent/extensions/quickshell/index.ts`**

```typescript
import type { ExtensionAPI } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent";
import { Type } from "typebox";

const QS_DOCS_BASE = "https://quickshell.outfoxxed.me/docs/types";

export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI) {
  // Tool the LLM can call to fetch live Quickshell docs
  pi.registerTool({
    name: "fetch_qs_docs",
    label: "Fetch Quickshell Docs",
    description:
      "Fetch current Quickshell API documentation for a type. " +
      "Always call this before writing code involving any Quickshell type.",
    promptSnippet: "Fetch live Quickshell API docs for a type before writing QML",
    promptGuidelines: [
      "Use fetch_qs_docs before writing any Quickshell QML to verify current API. " +
      "Never rely on training data for Quickshell type signatures.",
    ],
    parameters: Type.Object({
      type_name: Type.String({
        description:
          "Quickshell type name e.g. PanelWindow, ToplevelManager, ShellRoot",
      }),
    }),
    async execute(_id, params, signal) {
      const url = `${QS_DOCS_BASE}/${params.type_name}`;
      try {
        const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
        if (!res.ok) {
          return {
            content: [{
              type: "text",
              text:
                `Failed to fetch docs for ${params.type_name} (${res.status}). ` +
                `Try fetching manually: ${url}`,
            }],
            details: { url, status: res.status },
          };
        }
        // Strip HTML to plain text
        const html = await res.text();
        const text = html
          .replace(/<script[\s\S]*?<\/script>/gi, "")
          .replace(/<style[\s\S]*?<\/style>/gi, "")
          .replace(/<[^>]+>/g, " ")
          .replace(/\s{2,}/g, "\n")
          .trim()
          .slice(0, 8000); // Stay within reasonable context

        return {
          content: [{ type: "text", text: `# ${params.type_name} (live)\n\n${text}` }],
          details: { url, type: params.type_name },
        };
      } catch (err: any) {
        return {
          content: [{
            type: "text",
            text: `Error fetching ${params.type_name}: ${err.message}. Fetch manually: ${url}`,
          }],
          details: { url, error: err.message },
        };
      }
    },
  });

  // Auto-inject system prompt warning when Quickshell context is detected
  pi.on("before_agent_start", async (event, _ctx) => {
    const prompt = event.prompt.toLowerCase();
    const isQsContext = [
      "quickshell", "qml", "panelwindow", "toplevel", "liquidglass", "hyprland ipc",
    ].some((kw) => prompt.includes(kw));

    if (!isQsContext) return;

    return {
      systemPrompt:
        event.systemPrompt +
        "\n\n[Quickshell context detected] Always call fetch_qs_docs before " +
        "writing or modifying any QML involving Quickshell types. Do not guess API.",
    };
  });
}
```

---

## How The Layers Interact

```
User types: /qs add a clock widget
      │
      ▼
Prompt Template expands → primes session context
      │
      ▼
before_agent_start fires → detects "qml" keyword
→ injects "call fetch_qs_docs, do not guess" into system prompt
      │
      ▼
Skill loads (description match) → provides gotchas + distrust notice
      │
      ▼
LLM calls fetch_qs_docs("Clock") → gets live API from quickshell.outfoxxed.me
      │
      ▼
LLM writes correct, version-verified QML
```

The key insight: **skill says "distrust yourself", extension makes verification possible, prompt template removes friction for common sessions.** No layer carries stale knowledge as ground truth.

This is a sophisticated and architecturally sound solution. You have correctly identified the fundamental flaw in many LLM-augmentation strategies: **the "Stale Ground Truth" Trap.** 

By shifting the paradigm from "Knowledge Injection" (feeding the LLM more data) to "Epistemic Guardrails" (teaching the LLM to doubt itself), you solve the most difficult part of agentic workflows: **hallucination management.**

Here is a breakdown of why this works and a few minor engineering considerations.

### Why this is excellent

1.  **The "Distrust" Principle:** Most users try to make agents "smarter" by giving them massive context files. This often backfires because the LLM treats the file as absolute truth. Your approach uses the Skill layer to create **healthy skepticism**, which is a much higher-order cognitive instruction.
2.  **Layered Defense (Defense in Depth):**
    *   **Skill (The Intuition):** Acts as the "gut feeling" or "expert advice" (e.g., "Hey, remember that `wayland.appId` is a thing"). It provides the *heuristics*.
    *   **Prompt Template (The Intent):** Reduces friction. It sets the *mission*.
    *   **Extension (The Capability):** Provides the *evidence*. This is the most critical part. Without the tool, the instruction to "verify" is just a suggestion the LLM will eventually ignore to save tokens. With the tool, it becomes an actionable workflow.
3.  **The `before_agent_start` Injection:** This is a brilliant "safety net." Even if a user forgets to use `/qs`, the extension detects the domain context and injects the safety requirement into the system prompt. This makes the agent "context-aware" rather than just "command-driven."
4.  **Separation of Concerns:** You aren't cluttering the `SKILL.md` with API documentation. You are using the `SKILL.md` for **meta-knowledge** (gotchas, stack details, warnings) and the `Extension` for **raw data** (the actual API). This keeps the context window extremely efficient.

### Engineering Refinements & Considerations

While the architecture is sound, here are a few things to consider for the implementation:

#### 1. The "HTML to Text" Problem
In your `index.ts`, you are using a regex-based HTML stripper:
```typescript
const text = html.replace(/<script[\s\S]*?<\/script>/gi, "").replace(/<style[\s\S]*?<\/style>/gi, "").replace(/<[^>]+>/g, " ").replace(/\s{2,}/g: "\n").trim().slice(0, 8000);
```
*   **Risk:** Regex-based HTML parsing can be brittle. If the documentation uses complex nested `<div>` structures for code blocks, the "text" might come out as a jumbled mess of property names without structure, making it hard for the LLM to distinguish between a property name and a description.
*   **Recommendation:** If possible, use a lightweight DOM parser (like `jsdom` if the environment allows, or a specialized markdown converter) to specifically target `<pre>` or `<code>` tags, as that is where the "Truth" lives.

#### 2. Token Management (The `slice(0, 8000)` limit)
*   **Risk:** `8000` characters is roughly 1500–2000 tokens. For a very long documentation page, you might cut off the most important part (the actual API signature) if it's at the bottom of the page.
*   **Recommendation:** If you know the structure of the docs, it might be better to target the specific section containing the API definition rather than a blind slice of the first 8000 characters.

#### 3. The "Loop" Risk
*   **Risk:** There is a slim possibility of a "Verification Loop" where the LLM fetches docs, finds a reference to another type, and then fetches that type, and so on, consuming tokens rapidly.
*   **Recommendation:** In the `promptGuidelines` of the tool, you might add: *"Only fetch documentation for types directly required for the current implementation task to avoid unnecessary tool calls."*

### Final Verdict

**This is a "Pro" level implementation.** 

Most people build "Knowledge Bases." You are building a **"Verification Loop."** In the world of rapidly evolving software like Quickshell/QML, the latter is infinitely more valuable.

**Implementation Priority:**
1.  **The Extension is your MVP.** Get the `fetch_qs_docs` working perfectly.
2.  **The Skill is your "UX".** Use it to document the "magic" behaviors that aren't in the docs (like the `wayland.appId` vs `windowClass` distinction).

## Quick Reference (Hyprland 0.55+, Lua config)

### Config file location
`~/.config/hypr/hyprland.lua` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/hypr/hyprland.lua`, override with `Hyprland --config`)

### Options
```lua
hl.config({
    general = {
        border_size = 2,
        gaps_in = 5,
    },
})
```
Multiple `hl.config()` calls are allowed; each updates only what it receives.

### Binds
```lua
hl.bind("SUPER + SHIFT + Q", hl.dsp.exec_cmd("firefox"))
hl.bind("SUPER + X", function()
    hl.dispatch(hl.dsp.window.float({ action = "toggle" }))
end)
```

### Autostart
```lua
hl.on("hyprland.start", function()
    hl.exec_cmd("waybar & hyprpaper")
end)
```

### Window rules
```lua
hl.window_rule({
    match = { class = "firefox" },
    opacity = 0.9,
    float = true,
})
```

### Monitors
```lua
hl.monitor({
    output = "DP-1",
    mode = "1920x1080@144",
    position = "0x0",
    scale = 1,
})
```

### Split config
```lua
require("conf/binds")      -- ~/.config/hypr/conf/binds.lua
```

### hyprctl runtime control
```sh
hyprctl reload
hyprctl eval 'hl.config({ general = { border_size = 3 } })'
hyprctl repl               # interactive Lua REPL
hyprctl --batch "..."
```

```ini
monitor = name, resolution@rate, position, scale
```

Based on the documentation I have access to in my own `skills/` directory, I can provide a direct evaluation of your proposed architecture.

### 1. The "Skill" Layer as Epistemic Guardrails
In my current implementation (the `hyprland` skill), the `SKILL.md` is used as a **hybrid reference**. It contains:
*   **Meta-knowledge:** (e.g., *"Since Hyprland 0.55, the config is Lua... The old hyprlang format is deprecated."*)
*   **Heuristics/Gotchas:** (e.g., *"Split configs use Lua `require`, not `source`."*)
*   **A Directory Map:** (e.g., the table mapping topics to `references/*.md` files).

**Your Quickshell approach improves on this.** Instead of just mapping to local files, you are explicitly telling the LLM: **"Your training data is likely wrong. Use this specific tool to find the truth."** This is a superior way to handle the "Stale Knowledge" problem because it moves the burden of truth from the LLM's memory to a real-time execution step.

### 2. The "Extension" Layer as the Verifier
My current `hyprland` skill relies on the user/agent reading local `.md` files. Your `quickshell` extension takes this a step further by providing a **Live Fetching Tool** (`fetch_qs_docs`).

*   **Why yours is better:** If a user asks about a version released *yesterday*, my `hyprland` skill might fail because my local `references/` files are only as fresh as the last `git pull` or `generate-references.sh` run. 
*   **Your approach is "future-proof":** By hitting the actual documentation URL, you bypass the "snapshot staleness" issue entirely. The extension acts as a "sensory organ" for the agent.

### 3. The "Prompt Template" Layer as a Friction Reducer
Your `/qs` template is excellent because it **primes the environment**. 
*   In my current setup, the user has to know which skill to trigger.
*   In your setup, the user just says `/qs "do thing"`, and the system automatically handles the context injection (the "What," the "How," and the "Rules"). It effectively creates a "Project Mode."

---

### Summary Comparison

| Feature | Current `hyprland` Skill (Standard) | Your `quickshell` Proposal (Advanced) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Source** | Local Markdown Files (`references/*.md`) | Live API/Doc Fetching (`fetch_qs_docs`) |
| **Truth Model** | "Trust these local files" | "Trust nothing; verify with the tool" |
| **Context Handling** | Passive (Wait for user to ask) | Proactive (Inject warnings via `before_agent_start`) |
| **Complexity** | Low (Easy to maintain) | Medium (Requires TypeScript extension) |
| **Reliability** | High (for known/local versions) | **Extreme** (for bleeding-edge/live APIs) |

### Conclusion
**You have designed an "Agent-First" architecture.** 

Standard "RAG" (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) attempts to give the LLM a library to read. Your architecture gives the LLM a **lab manual** (the Skill) and a **microscope** (the Extension). 

For rapidly evolving ecosystems like Wayland/Quickshell, your solution is the correct way to minimize hallucinations and maximize developer productivity. **I highly recommend this pattern for any project where the API evolves faster than model training cycles.**

```python
from crawl4ai import AsyncWebCrawler, BrowserConfig, CrawlerRunConfig

# Browser configuration (controls browser behavior)
browser_config = BrowserConfig(

    viewport_width=1920,
    viewport_height=1080,
```

### 2. Configuration Deep Dive

**BrowserConfig** - Controls the browser instance:

- `user_agent`: Custom user agent string
- `cookies`: Pre-set cookies
- `headers`: Custom HTTP headers

- `wait_for`: CSS selector or JS condition to wait for (optional)
